interactions.label: A woman who dies from injuries sustained in a road traffic accident at 36 weeks

params.question: A woman who dies from injuries sustained in a road traffic accident at 36 weeks of pregnancy is classified as a maternal death.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. The WHO definition requires the cause of death to be related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management. Deaths from accidental or incidental causes — such as a road traffic accident — are explicitly excluded. They do not enter either the direct or indirect obstetric death category.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The WHO definition specifies that a maternal death must be caused by or related to the pregnancy or its management. Accidental or incidental causes such as road traffic injuries are explicitly excluded, even if the woman was pregnant at the time of death.

interactions.label: A pregnant woman develops severe postpartum haemorrhage in a remote village. Her

params.question: A pregnant woman develops severe postpartum haemorrhage in a remote village. Her family recognises the danger and calls an ambulance immediately, but it takes three hours to arrive due to poor roads. She reaches the district hospital alive but dies because no blood is available for transfusion. Which delays from the Thaddeus-Maine model contributed to this death?

answers.text: Delay I only — the family failed to recognise the danger signs in time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The scenario states the family recognised the danger and called an ambulance immediately. There was no delay in deciding to seek care (Delay I).

answers.text: Delay II only — the ambulance took three hours due to poor roads

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While Delay II (reaching a facility) was present due to geographic isolation, the absence of blood at the hospital is a separate failure — Delay III (receiving adequate care at the facility).

answers.text: Delays II and III — delayed transport to the facility and inadequate care on arrival

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The three-hour journey represents Delay II (reaching a facility), caused by geographic isolation and poor roads. The lack of blood for transfusion represents Delay III (receiving adequate care at the facility). Most Indian maternal deaths involve more than one delay simultaneously.

answers.text: Delays I, II, and III — all three delays contributed to this death

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delay I is a delay in deciding to seek care, often due to failure to recognise danger signs or financial barriers. Here the family acted immediately — no Delay I occurred. Only Delays II (transport) and III (facility care) contributed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three delays model: Delay I = deciding to seek care, Delay II = reaching a facility, Delay III = receiving adequate care at the facility. In this case the family acted promptly (no Delay I), but the ambulance took hours (Delay II) and the hospital lacked blood (Delay III).
Well done. Identifying which specific delays apply is the first step in a structured maternal death review, guiding targeted interventions at the community, transport, or facility level.

params.question: You are setting up a caesarean section audit at your district hospital using the Robson classification. A colleague suggests recording only the mode of delivery and maternal age for each patient. What essential obstetric information would this approach fail to capture?

answers.text: Blood group, Rh status, and maternal haemoglobin level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are important clinical parameters, but they are not among the six characteristics used in the Robson classification. The system uses purely obstetric variables to sort patients into its ten mutually exclusive groups.

answers.text: Fetal presentation, onset of labour, and previous caesarean section history

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Robson system classifies every delivery using six obstetric characteristics: parity, previous caesarean section, fetal presentation, onset of labour (spontaneous, induced, or pre-labour caesarean), gestational age, and number of fetuses. Neither mode of delivery nor maternal age is a classification variable.

answers.text: Neonatal birth weight, Apgar scores, and NICU admission status

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are neonatal outcome measures, not classification inputs. The Robson system classifies patients prospectively using maternal and obstetric characteristics known before or at the time of delivery.

answers.text: Surgeon's experience level, duration of surgery, and anaesthesia type

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are operative details, not Robson classification variables. The system groups patients by obstetric profile — parity, previous caesarean, presentation, labour onset, gestational age, and fetal number — not by surgical factors.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Robson Ten-Group Classification uses six obstetric characteristics: parity, previous caesarean section, fetal presentation, onset of labour, gestational age, and number of fetuses. Maternal age and mode of delivery are not classification parameters.
Exactly. Accurate Robson classification depends on prospective recording of all six obstetric parameters at the time of delivery — a clinical responsibility, not an administrative one.

params.question: A pregnant woman delivers at a government hospital and receives a direct cash payment afterwards. Her ASHA worker also receives a separate incentive for facilitating the institutional delivery. Under which national programme were these cash transfers made?

answers.text: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) — which provides free delivery and newborn care services

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: JSSK (2011) removes costs by making delivery, drugs, diagnostics, blood transfusions, meals, and transport entirely free. It does not provide cash payments — it eliminates out-of-pocket expenditure.

answers.text: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) — which provides conditional cash transfers for institutional delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. JSY, launched in 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission, is a conditional cash transfer scheme. Both the mother and the ASHA worker receive cash incentives for institutional delivery. This scheme is credited with raising India's institutional delivery rate from around 40% in 2005 to over 80% by the mid-2010s.

answers.text: Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN) — which guarantees respectful maternity care

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SUMAN (2019) guarantees respectful, dignified, free care with specific entitlements such as four antenatal visits, a skilled birth attendant, and 48-hour postnatal care. It is a rights and quality guarantee built on top of JSSK's free services, not a cash transfer programme.

answers.text: Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) — which provides iron and folic acid supplementation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: AMB (2018) is a national strategy to reduce anaemia using a 6×6×6 framework — six beneficiary groups, six interventions, and six institutional mechanisms. It provides supplementation and deworming, not cash transfers.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the core mechanism of each programme: JSY (2005) = cash transfer for institutional delivery, JSSK (2011) = free services including delivery, drugs, blood, and transport, AMB (2018) = anaemia reduction through the 6×6×6 framework, SUMAN (2019) = rights guarantee for respectful, free care.

Well identified. JSY is India's cash incentive scheme; JSSK removes costs; SUMAN guarantees rights and quality. Knowing which programme applies to which entitlement is part of your clinical responsibility.
